---
title: "Strand C · Approved drugs"
subtitle: "Clinical pharmacology as the regulator actually saw it"
---

Strands `P`, `S` and `D` teach ideas: what a drug does to a receptor, how to
estimate a parameter, what a disease does to a model. Strand `C` teaches
something different — **what happened when someone had to convince a regulator**.

Every approved drug carries a public record of an argument that was made and
adjudicated: a dose was proposed, a model was fitted, a reviewer agreed or did
not, and a number went into a label that now governs how the drug is given to
patients. That record is the closest thing this field has to a worked-answer
key, and it is almost entirely unread outside the industry.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## The inclusion test
A drug earns a place here only if its review shows **a modelling decision doing
work that could have gone the other way**. A clean, uncontested development
programme teaches nothing that strand `S` does not teach better. What is wanted
is the drug where the model replaced a trial, or where the model was overruled,
or where the analysis was fine and the conclusion was still wrong.
:::

## Why these sources are different

Everything in [Reading](reading.qmd) is copyrighted literature that this project
can link to and never reproduce. FDA review documents are not. They are works of
the United States Government, and are in the **public domain**.

That single fact changes what strand `C` can be. For the first time in this
curriculum, the numbers underlying a lesson — clearance estimates, covariate
coefficients, exposure–response slopes — can be transcribed into a CSV, committed
to the repository, and reproduced by anyone, without a licence question. The
lessons in `P` and `S` teach methods on simulated data because that is all they
may use. `C` does not have that constraint.

The standing rules still hold: no PDF is committed, no figure is copied, and
every transcribed row carries its source document and page so a reader can check
the transcription against the original.

comparators, and repeating it here would split one discussion across two strands.

## Two findings from building this outline

Both came out of checking sources rather than reading about them, and both change
what the lessons can claim.

### The machine-readable route is real, and it lies by default

The **openFDA** label API returns structured JSON, and for sotorasib it carries
`clinical_pharmacology`, `pharmacodynamics` and `pharmacokinetics` as separate
fields — enough to build a notebook that needs nothing committed and never goes
stale.

The trap is that an unfiltered query returns whichever label ranks first, and for
both PD-1 antibodies that is now the recently approved **subcutaneous
coformulation** — `KEYTRUDA QLEX`, `OPDIVO QVANTIG` — not the intravenous product
the modelling literature describes. Querying `openfda.generic_name:"pembrolizumab"`
silently hands back a different drug's label. Adding `_exists_:pharmacokinetics`
fixes the missing-field symptom without fixing the wrong-product cause. Any
notebook in this strand pins the specific SPL and asserts on the brand name before
parsing a single number.

### Cell and gene therapy has no clinical pharmacology review to read

[Kymriah](https://www.fda.gov/vaccines-blood-biologics/cellular-gene-therapy-products/kymriah-tisagenlecleucel)'s
public document set is the package insert, the approval letters, a Summary Basis
for Regulatory Action, a statistical review, a clinical memo and a REMS. There is
no clinical pharmacology review and no multi-discipline review, because CBER's
review pathway does not produce one.

This is the structural explanation for the gap the [Resources](resources.qmd)
page found empirically — gene therapy has seven regulatory guidances in the
database and zero runnable open models. It is not that the modelling is being
done and withheld. For this product class the document that strand `C` is built
on does not exist. `C-12` is that lesson, and it is the reason the strand ends
with a product it cannot analyse the way it analyses the other eleven.

## The source material, verified

Every reference below was retrieved and checked through **PubMed** — title,
journal, year, authors and DOI. Full entries are on the [Reading](reading.qmd)
page under *Strand C*.

**A model instead of a trial.** Lala et al., Eur J Cancer 2020
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2020.02.016)) is the pembrolizumab Q6W
analysis: a population model built on 2,993 subjects across five trials, used to
show that 400 mg every six weeks produces a geometric mean average concentration
about 1% above the established 200 mg every three weeks, with peak concentrations
roughly 65% below the highest dose ever given clinically. Efficacy and safety
were bridged by exposure alone. Note the corrigendum
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2020.12.006)) — `C-02` cites both, because
a lesson about careful reading should not misquote its own source.

**Flat exposure–response.** Zhao et al., Br J Clin Pharmacol 2024
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1111/bcp.16188)) analysed 1,493 subjects for
pharmacokinetics and 756 from CheckMate 577 for exposure–response, and found the
hazard ratios at the 5th and 95th exposure percentiles were similar for both
disease-free survival and grade ≥2 immune-mediated adverse events. `C-03` is
about what that symmetry does and does not permit you to conclude.

**The dose nobody defended.** Ratain, Tannock and Lichter, J Clin Oncol 2021
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.21.01371)) — *Dose Optimization of Sotorasib:
Is the US Food and Drug Administration Sending a Message?* Three pages, and the
sharpest regulatory argument in this reading list.

**Exposure–response as a trade, quantified.** Hanley et al., Clin Pharmacol Ther
2023 ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/cpt.2956)) modelled the OPTIC dose-ranging
study with a four-state discrete-time Markov model for molecular response and
time-to-event models for harm. A 15 mg dose increase carried an odds ratio of
2.05 (95% CI 1.53–2.89) for one molecular response transition — and a hazard
ratio of 2.05 (95% CI 1.43–2.93) for arterial occlusive events. The same
coefficient, for the benefit and for the harm. `C-05` exists because of that
coincidence.

**When PK stops predicting PD.** Luo et al., J Clin Lipidol 2023
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacl.2023.04.010)) reported a single
subcutaneous dose of inclisiran with an elimination half-life of **6.5 hours**
and LDL-C still reduced by 49.6% (100 mg) and 58.3% (300 mg) at **day 90**.
Barkas and Ray, Expert Opin Pharmacother 2024
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1080/14656566.2024.2337253)) place that alongside the
PCSK9 antibodies. Roughly three orders of magnitude separate the exposure
timescale from the effect timescale, and `C-08` is about what a modeller does
with that.

**Dose as a schedule.** Guo et al., Clin Transl Sci 2024
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1111/cts.13717), free full text) describe teclistamab's
1.5 mg/kg weekly maintenance reached through step-up doses of 0.06 and 0.3 mg/kg,
selected on exposure–response for both efficacy and safety.

**Liposomal exposure, in pancreatic cancer.** Brendel et al., CPT Pharmacometrics
Syst Pharmacol 2021 ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12725), free full text)
built a population model on 440 patients across seven studies, with
exposure–safety analyses in metastatic PDAC from NAPOLI-1. Total irinotecan
clearance 0.107 L/h against SN-38 clearance 118 L/h; UGT1A1\*28 7/7 homozygosity
had no significant effect on SN-38 clearance — a negative covariate result worth
more teaching time than a positive one. This paper is shared with `D1-08`.

**Why C-12 is different.** Belov et al., CPT Pharmacometrics Syst Pharmacol 2021
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12597), free full text), written by FDA CBER
staff, sets out the opportunities and challenges for model-informed drug
development in gene therapies. It is the authors of the gap describing the gap.

**Modelling that did not win.** Desborough et al., Ann Biomed Eng 2022
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10439-022-03062-4)) document an MIDD pilot
submission for an Afrezza label change in which FDA accepted the simulation as
informative and still asked for conventional clinical evidence. A published
account of a modelling argument that was found credible and was not sufficient —
rare, and useful.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## What this outline is not evidence of
Thirteen verified applications and twenty-one verified papers are not thirteen
written lessons. The application records were retrieved and confirmed; the **review
documents themselves have not been read**. Every claim above about what a review
*shows* is a hypothesis drawn from the published literature and the approval
history, and each one has to survive contact with the actual document before it
becomes a lesson. Where it does not survive, the correction gets written down —
as happened with van der Graaf on the [Reading](reading.qmd) page.
:::

## What comes next

`C-02` on pembrolizumab is the natural first lesson: the exposure-matching
argument is self-contained, the supporting paper is unusually clear, and the
conclusion — that a regimen entered the label without an efficacy trial — is
striking enough to carry a reader who does not yet care about population models.

`C-08` on inclisiran is the strongest second, because the PK/PD disconnect breaks
the intuition that strand `S` spends its early lessons building, and breaking a
freshly built intuition is when it is cheapest to repair.

The runnable component is planned in two halves, per the design decision behind
this strand: a notebook that queries the openFDA label API live — pinned to a
specific SPL, for the reasons above — and a small committed CSV of parameters
transcribed from the public-domain review documents, each row carrying its source
document and page. Neither exists yet.
